units.title: Hello, R
units.summary: Write your first R code: print values, show text with cat() and calculate with numbers.

lesson.md: R is a programming language for data and statistics. A program is a list of instructions that R runs from top to bottom. The function `print()` shows a value on the screen. Text goes in double quotes: `"Hello, R!"` is a **string**.

lesson.code: print("Hello, R!")

lesson.md: The `[1]` at the start of the line is the position of the first value on that line. In R, even a single value is stored as a **vector**, a sequence of values, here with only one element. You learn more about vectors in unit 3. `print()` also shows strings with their quotes.

lesson.code:
print(42)
print(3.5)
print("R")

lesson.md: The function `cat()` writes text as it is, without `[1]` and without quotes. It does not end the line by itself, so you add `"\n"`, the **newline** character, at the end. When you give `cat()` several values, separated by commas, it puts a space between them.

lesson.code:
cat("Hello, R!\n")
cat("I am", 30, "years old\n")
lesson.output:
Hello, R!
I am 30 years old

lesson.md: R can calculate. `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies, `/` divides and `^` raises to a power. `%%` gives the remainder of a division, and `%/%` divides and drops the remainder. As in mathematics, `^` comes first, then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-`. Parentheses change the order.

lesson.code:
print(7 + 3)
print(7 / 2)
print(2 ^ 10)
print(7 %% 3)
print(7 %/% 3)
print((1 + 2) * 4)

lesson.md: A **comment** starts with `#`. R ignores everything from `#` to the end of the line. In this course, comments only show results, like `# 6` below.

lesson.code: print(2 * 3)  # 6

lesson.md: R is case-sensitive: `print` and `Print` are different names. `Print("Hi")` stops with the error `could not find function "Print"`.

card: `cat("Hi\n")` writes text without quotes; `"\n"` ends the line

`%/%` drops the remainder, so the result is `3`. `7 / 2` would give `3.5`.

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, get to know numeric, character and logical values, and join text with paste().

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name that stores a value. In R you create one with `<-`, the assignment arrow: a less-than sign followed by a minus. Read `age <- 30` as "age gets 30". You can give a variable a new value later, even one that uses its old value.

lesson.code:
age <- 30
print(age)
age <- age + 1
print(age)

lesson.md: A name can contain letters, digits, `.` and `_`, and it starts with a letter: `price`, `total_2`, `first.name`. Names are case-sensitive, so `age` and `Age` are two different variables. `=` also works for assignment, but most R code uses `<-`.
Every value has a type. Numbers are `numeric`, text in quotes is `character`, and the two values `TRUE` and `FALSE` are `logical`. The function `class()` tells you the type of a value.

lesson.code:
price <- 9.99
name <- "Ana"
ready <- TRUE
print(class(price))
print(class(name))
print(class(ready))

lesson.md: Whole numbers are `numeric` too. If you need a real whole-number type, add `L` after the number: `5L` is an `integer`. Most of the time, `numeric` is all you need.

lesson.code:
print(class(5))
print(class(5L))

lesson.md: `paste()` joins values into one string and puts a space between them. `paste0()` joins them without a space. Numbers are turned into text automatically.

lesson.code:
name <- "Ana"
age <- 30
greeting <- paste("Hi,", name)
print(greeting)
print(paste0(name, age))
cat(name, "is", age, "years old\n")

lesson.md: `nchar()` counts the characters of a string, and `toupper()` writes it in capital letters. `as.numeric()` turns text like `"2.5"` into a number, and `as.character()` turns a number into text.

lesson.code:
print(nchar("banana"))
print(toupper("r is fun"))
x <- as.numeric("2.5")
print(x * 2)
print(as.character(42))

lesson.md: You cannot calculate with text. `"5" + 1` stops with the error `non-numeric argument to binary operator`. Convert the text first: `as.numeric("5") + 1` is `6`.

card: `paste("a", "b")` gives `"a b"`; `paste0()` joins without a space

units.title: Vectors
units.summary: Keep many values in one vector, create sequences, pick elements by position and calculate with all elements at once.

lesson.md: A **vector** holds several values of the same type, in order. The function `c()` combines values into a vector. `print()` shows all elements on one line.

lesson.code:
prices <- c(4, 8, 15)
print(prices)
fruits <- c("apple", "mango")
print(fruits)

lesson.md: Now the `[1]` makes sense: a single value is a vector with one element. `length()` gives the number of elements of a vector.

lesson.code:
x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)
print(length(x))
print(length(7))

lesson.md: `1:5` creates the whole numbers from 1 to 5. It also counts down: `10:7`. For other steps, use `seq()` with a start, an end and the step `by`.

lesson.code:
print(1:5)
print(10:7)
print(seq(0, 20, by = 5))

lesson.md: Square brackets pick elements by position. R counts from 1, so `x[1]` is the first element. A vector of positions picks several elements, and a negative position removes that element.

lesson.code:
fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")
print(fruits[1])
print(fruits[3])
print(fruits[c(1, 3)])
print(fruits[-2])

lesson.md: `x[0]` is not the first element: it gives an empty vector. A position after the end, like `x[10]` for a vector of three elements, gives `NA`, which means "missing value".

Arithmetic works on every element at once: `prices * 2` doubles each price. Two vectors of the same length are combined element by element. `sum()`, `mean()`, `max()` and `min()` summarize a whole vector.

lesson.code:
prices <- c(4, 8, 15)
print(prices * 2)
print(prices + c(1, 2, 3))
print(sum(prices))
print(mean(prices))
print(max(prices))

lesson.md: A vector has one type only. If you mix types, `c()` converts everything to one type: `c(1, "a")` becomes the character vector `"1" "a"`.

card: `x[1]` is the first element; `x[-1]` removes it

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Compare values, run code only when a condition is TRUE with if and else, and test whole vectors with ifelse().

lesson.md: A **comparison** gives a logical value, `TRUE` or `FALSE`. `==` means equal (two equals signs), `!=` means not equal, and `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` compare sizes.

lesson.code:
x <- 7
print(x > 5)
print(x == 10)
print(x != 10)

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `TRUE`. The condition goes in parentheses, and the code goes in curly braces `{ }`. `else` adds code for the case `FALSE`. Write `else` on the same line as the closing brace: `} else {`.
`else if` checks another condition when the ones before it were `FALSE`. R checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch that matches.
If `else` starts a new line after the closing brace `}`, R thinks the `if` is already finished and stops with the error `unexpected 'else'`.
`&&` means **and**: both conditions must be `TRUE`. `||` means **or**: at least one must be `TRUE`. `!` means **not**: it turns `TRUE` into `FALSE` and the other way round.

A comparison with a vector compares every element and gives a logical vector. Inside square brackets, it keeps the elements where the result is `TRUE`. `&` and `|` combine logical vectors element by element. `ifelse(test, yes, no)` picks a value for every element.

lesson.code:
scores <- c(45, 80, 62, 30)
print(scores >= 50)
print(scores[scores >= 50])
print(scores > 40 & scores < 70)
print(ifelse(scores >= 50, "pass", "fail"))
lesson.output:
[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
[1] 80 62
[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE
[1] "fail" "pass" "pass" "fail"

lesson.md: Use `&&` and `||` in `if`, where you need exactly one `TRUE` or `FALSE`. Use `&` and `|` when you work with whole vectors.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for and while, loop over positions with seq_along(), and learn when vectorized code is better.

lesson.md: A `for` loop runs the same code once for every element of a vector. In `for (fruit in fruits)`, the variable `fruit` holds the next element in each round.

lesson.output:
apple is tasty
banana is tasty
cherry is tasty

lesson.md: A loop often builds a result step by step. Start with a value before the loop, then change it in every round. Here `total` starts at 0 and grows by each number.

When you need the position of each element, loop over `seq_along(v)`. It gives the positions `1, 2, 3, ...` of `v`. It is safer than `1:length(v)`, because for an empty vector `1:length(v)` gives `1 0` and the loop runs anyway.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `TRUE`. Make sure that something in the loop changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
`break` stops a loop immediately. `next` skips the rest of the current round and continues with the next one.

Many loops in R can be replaced by one vectorized expression. Both programs below double every price, but `prices * 2` is shorter and usually much faster. In the same way, `sum(x)` replaces a loop that adds up `x`.

lesson.code:
prices <- c(4, 8, 15)
doubled <- c()
for (p in prices) {
  doubled <- c(doubled, p * 2)
}
print(doubled)
print(prices * 2)

lesson.md: Use vectorized code when you do the same thing to every element. Use a loop when each step depends on the step before, like the `while` loop that doubles `n`.

card: `for (x in v) { ... }` runs once for every element
`for (i in seq_along(v))` loops over the positions
`break` stops the loop, `next` skips a round

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with function(), pass arguments, give them default values and return results.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named piece of code that you can use again and again. You create one with `function()` and store it in a variable with `<-`. The names in the parentheses are the **arguments**: the values the function receives.
A function gives back a **return value**: the value of the last line in its body. You can store it in a variable or use it in a calculation.
`return(value)` leaves the function immediately and gives back `value`. This is useful when a function can stop early.

Separate several arguments with commas. Write `= value` after an argument to give it a **default**: R uses it when the caller leaves the argument out. When you call a function, you can also name the arguments, like `by = 5` in `seq(0, 20, by = 5)`. Named arguments can come in any order.
Inside `function()`, `=` sets a default. In a call, `=` names an argument. For normal variables, keep using `<-`.
Because arithmetic works on whole vectors, many functions work on vectors without any extra code. The function below converts one temperature or a whole vector of temperatures.
Variables that you create inside a function are **local**: they exist only while the function runs. After the call, R does not know them, and using them gives the error `object not found`.

card: The last value is returned; `return(v)` leaves early

units.title: Lists and apply
units.summary: Group values of different types in a list, use names and $, and apply a function to every element with sapply() and lapply().

lesson.md: A vector holds values of one type. A **list** can hold values of different types, even whole vectors. You create it with `list()`. Give each element a name with `name = value`, and get it back with `$` and the name.

lesson.code:
person <- list(name = "Ana", age = 30, langs = c("R", "Python"))
print(person$name)
print(person$age + 1)
print(person$langs)

lesson.md: Double square brackets `[[ ]]` also get an element, by position or by name in quotes. `names()` gives the names of all elements, and `length()` gives the number of elements.

lesson.code:
person <- list(name = "Ana", year = 1994)
print(names(person))
print(person[["year"]])
print(person[[1]])
print(length(person))

lesson.md: To change an element, assign a new value with `$` and `<-`. If the name does not exist yet, R adds a new element to the list.

lesson.code:
person <- list(name = "Ana")
person$city <- "Rome"
person$name <- "Ana Lima"
print(names(person))
print(person$name)

lesson.md: Single brackets on a list, like `person[1]`, give a smaller list, not the element itself. Use `person[[1]]` or `person$name` to get the value.

lesson.text: Applying a function to every element

lesson.md: `sapply(x, f)` calls the function `f` once for every element of `x` and collects the results in a vector. Write the function name without parentheses: `sapply(x, mean)`, not `sapply(x, mean())`.

lesson.code:
scores <- list(c(7, 9), c(4, 6, 8), 10)
print(sapply(scores, mean))
print(sapply(scores, length))

lesson.md: You can also write a small function directly inside the call, like `function(n) n * 10`. `lapply()` works like `sapply()`, but it always gives back a list.

lesson.code:
nums <- c(1, 2, 3)
print(sapply(nums, function(n) n * 10))
squares <- lapply(nums, function(n) n ^ 2)
print(squares[[2]])
print(class(squares))

lesson.md: For simple arithmetic, vectorized code like `nums * 10` is easier. `sapply()` is useful when each element is itself a vector, as in the list of scores.

card: `sapply(x, f)` gives a vector, `lapply(x, f)` a list

units.title: Data frames
units.summary: Store tables in data frames, get columns with $, pick rows and columns with [ , ] and calculate with whole columns.

lesson.md: A **data frame** is a table. Each column is a vector with a name, and all columns have the same length. You create one with `data.frame(column = vector, ...)`. `print()` shows the table with row numbers on the left.

lesson.code:
people <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"),
  age = c(28, 35, 42),
  city = c("Rome", "Oslo", "Lima")
)
print(people)
lesson.output:
name age city
1  Ana  28 Rome
2  Ben  35 Oslo
3 Cleo  42 Lima

lesson.md: `nrow()` gives the number of rows, `ncol()` the number of columns, and `names()` the column names.

lesson.code:
people <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"),
  age = c(28, 35, 42),
  city = c("Rome", "Oslo", "Lima")
)
print(nrow(people))
print(ncol(people))
print(names(people))

lesson.md: `$` and the column name give you a column as a vector. Everything you know about vectors works on it, like `mean()` and `max()`.

lesson.code:
people <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"),
  age = c(28, 35, 42),
  city = c("Rome", "Oslo", "Lima")
)
print(people$age)
print(mean(people$age))
print(max(people$age))

lesson.md: Square brackets with a comma pick rows and columns: `people[row, column]`. Leave one side empty to get all of it: `people[1, ]` is the whole first row, and `people[, "city"]` is the whole column `city`. You can use numbers or column names.

lesson.code:
people <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"),
  age = c(28, 35, 42),
  city = c("Rome", "Oslo", "Lima")
)
print(people[2, "name"])
print(people[1, ])
print(people[, "city"])

lesson.md: A condition on a column gives `TRUE` or `FALSE` for every row. Put it before the comma to keep only the matching rows.

lesson.code:
people <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"),
  age = c(28, 35, 42),
  city = c("Rome", "Oslo", "Lima")
)
older <- people[people$age > 30, ]
print(older)
print(nrow(older))
lesson.output:
name age city
2  Ben  35 Oslo
3 Cleo  42 Lima
[1] 2

lesson.md: To add a column, assign a vector to a new name with `$` and `<-`. Vectorized arithmetic calculates the new value for every row at once.

lesson.code:
people <- data.frame(name = c("Ana", "Ben"), age = c(28, 35))
people$months <- people$age * 12
print(people)

lesson.md: Do not forget the comma. `people[2, ]` is the second row, but `people[2]` is the second column, as a small data frame.

exercises.code:
df <- data.frame(item = c("pen", "cup", "bag"), price = c(2, 6, 10))
print(df[df$price > 5, "item"])
exercises.explain: The condition keeps the rows with a price above 5, which are cup and bag, and `"item"` picks that column.

exercises.prompt: Which code gives the second row of the data frame `df`?
exercises.explain: The row comes before the comma. `df[, 2]` and `df[2]` give the second column, and `df$2` is not valid.

exercises.code:
df <- data.frame(a = c(5, 6), b = c(7, 8))
print(df[1, "b"])
exercises.explain: Row 1 of column `b` is the first value of `b`, which is 7.
